body.heading: Copies all the way down
paragraphs: Break a floret off a romanesco cauliflower and it looks like a miniature cauliflower, complete with its own smaller florets, which have smaller ones still. Shapes that resemble themselves at every scale are called fractals, and nature is full of them: fern leaves, tree branches, river deltas, lightning bolts and the branching of blood vessels all repeat their pattern as you zoom.

Mathematicians build exact fractals with simple rules repeated forever. Start with a triangle, add a smaller triangle to the middle of each side, then repeat - you get the Koch snowflake, a shape whose edge gets longer at every step without limit, while the area inside stays modest and finite.

body.heading: The coastline that would not sit still
paragraphs: In the 1950s the scientist Lewis Fry Richardson noticed something odd: the measured length of a coastline depends on the length of your ruler. A long ruler strides past bays and inlets; a short one follows them, and a shorter one still traces every rock. Britain's coast measures roughly twice as long with a short ruler as with a long one - and in principle it never settles to one true value.

Coastlines are fractal-like, so the question 'how long is the coast?' is incomplete until you add 'measured at what scale?' It is a cheerful warning that some quantities depend on how you look, and that more precision does not always mean more truth.

body.heading: Try it yourself
paragraphs: Draw the first three stages of a Koch snowflake: begin with a triangle, then replace the middle third of each side with two sides of a smaller outward triangle, and repeat on the new, wigglier shape. Count the sides each time - the count multiplies by four at every stage.

Or take a map of a wiggly coastline or river and 'measure' it twice: once with long straight steps on a ruler, once with short steps of a compass or a piece of string. Compare the two answers and you have reproduced Richardson's discovery at home.

takeaway: Fractals repeat their pattern at every scale, which is why zooming in never simplifies them - and why some lengths depend on your ruler.
